title: Pass the blame back, add it up
allegory: Backprop is a kitchen inquest run backwards from the judge's score: each cook waits until every dish they fed into has sent back a note saying how much the score moves per unit of their ingredient, adds those notes up, and only then sends notes on to their own suppliers.
map: the judge's score on the final dish
the loss L, the root of the graph
a note: how much the score moves per unit of what you supplied
the gradient arriving along one edge, dL/d(node)
wait until every dish you fed into has reported
topological order: every consumer runs its backward before the node does
add up the notes from every dish you supplied
accumulate: dL/da is the sum over all paths from a to L
the farm at the end of the chain files the final tally
leaf tensors: the gradient is written into .grad
credit: Accumulate-don't-overwrite bug and the topological walk framed as in Andrej Karpathy's micrograd video, The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation.
where_else: loss.backward() in every training loop: this exact walk, done for you by autograd
Build systems and spreadsheets: compute a cell only once everything it depends on is ready
Gradient-based attribution in interpretability: the same backward walk from a logit to an activation

hamming.what: Getting every weight's gradient in one backward sweep, walking the graph from the loss outwards so each node's incoming gradient is complete, and adding where a value was used twice.
hamming.when: Every time you call loss.backward(); you build it by hand once in [0.4], then let autograd do it forever after.
hamming.why: Nudging each weight and re-running the model needs one full run per weight; backprop gets them all from one forward and one backward pass.

object.title: The blame relay
object.subtitle: A small computation graph where pulses of gradient run from the loss back to the weights, adding up where paths meet.

cap.1: Every step of the calculation left a node, with a link back to what it was made from. The loss sits at the root.
cap.2: The forward pass records a recipe per tensor: which op made it and from which parents. That record is the graph backprop walks.
cap.3: A DAG of recorded ops: each non-leaf holds its function, args and parents. L is the root; parameters and inputs are the leaves.

cap.1: Blame starts at the loss and flows back. A node may only pass it on once everyone who used it has reported in.
cap.2: Topologically sort from L outwards, then walk that order. Each node's backward turns grad-wrt-output into grad-wrt-each-input.
cap.3: Topological order guarantees every consumer has deposited its contribution before a node's backward runs; violate it and a partial grad propagates silently.

cap.1: a was used twice, by f and by the plus. Two notes of blame arrive, and a must add them. Keep only one and you often get exactly half.
cap.2: Fan-out means one gradient per path, and the answer is their sum. Assign instead of add and d(x·x)/dx comes out as x, not 2x.
cap.3: dL/da = dL/dc · (1 + f'(a)): the identity path plus the branch. Accumulate with +=; addition commutes, so sibling order does not matter.

cap.1: At the far end, the weight files its tally. That number is what the optimiser will use to take a step.
cap.2: At leaves, the gradient is written into .grad instead of being passed further. Backprop fills .grad; the optimiser decides what to do with it.
cap.3: Leaves with requires_grad get .grad written; intermediate grads are held temporarily. Broadcast ops need unbroadcast: sum over stretched dims.

cap.1: One walk back gives every weight its number at once. Nudging each weight one at a time would need a whole new run per weight.
cap.2: Finite differences need a forward pass per parameter, fine only as a check. Backprop gets all gradients from one forward and one backward pass.
cap.3: Reverse-mode AD suits one scalar output and many inputs. Check against central differences on a small function: no shared failure mode.

predict.q: In c = a + f(a), a feeds both f and the plus. What is dL/da?

options.t: The sum of the gradients from both paths

predict.why: Each path carries its own share of a's influence on L, and the chain rule adds them. Overwriting keeps one term of a two-term sum.

predict.q: Your backprop matches PyTorch on a straight chain but gives exactly half on x * x. Most likely bug?

options.t: Assigning each gradient instead of adding it

predict.why: x * x uses x twice, and each use sends back x. The true gradient is x + x = 2x; overwriting keeps only one x.

predict.q: Why sort the graph before walking it?

options.t: So each node's incoming gradient is complete before its backward runs
To make the forward pass faster
So the leaves are processed first

predict.why: Run a node early and it passes on a partial gradient. Nothing errors; the numbers are just quietly too small.

object.where: Any dependency graph handled in reverse order: autograd engines, build systems, spreadsheet recalculation.
